title: Security review: Dedicated provisioning (image provenance, audit logs, change management)
summary: Harborview reviewed Redwood’s Dedicated capacity bring-up process with a focus on (1) golden image provenance and promotion controls, (2) audit logging for provisioning actions and break-glass overrides, and (3) change-management expectations (advance notice, maintenance windows, and rollback). Redwood walked through the in-flight “provision-to-ready” automation work: versioned images, artifact signing/SBOM, RBAC + least privilege on the provisioning service, and stage-level readiness gates before routing. Customer requested concrete evidence examples (sample audit log events, signing verification, and change log entries), plus clarity on who at Redwood can trigger provisioning and how those actions are approved.
topics: Golden image pipeline (drivers, OS hardening) and promotion flow
Artifact provenance: signing, SBOMs, build attestations
Audit logs: who triggered provisioning runs, stage transitions, overrides
RBAC and least privilege for provisioning service + operators
Change management: notifications, maintenance windows, rollback criteria
Data residency / region constraints and access controls
Readiness gates and ‘Ready’ semantics before entering routing
questions: Customer asked: Do you sign images and provide SBOMs? Can we validate signatures independently? What gets logged for provisioning (who/what/when) and can logs be exported to our SIEM? Is there a formal approval step before capacity changes? What is your break-glass process and is it audited/alerted? How do you handle emergency changes vs scheduled changes? Who has access to the underlying hosts in Dedicated?
action_items: Redwood (Kevin Osei): Send sample audit log payloads for provisioning events (trigger/run ID, stage start/finish, Ready marking, break-glass usage) by 2025-03-10.
Redwood (Marcus Lin): Share image provenance details (signing method, SBOM format, attestation approach) and current hardening checklist excerpt by 2025-03-10.
Customer (Dina Patel): Confirm Harborview’s required log export mechanism (Splunk HEC vs syslog vs S3) and retention expectations by 2025-03-12.
Redwood (Lauren Bishop): Propose a change-management template for Dedicated capacity expansions (notice period, maintenance window, rollback criteria) by 2025-03-13.
Both: Schedule a 30-min follow-up with Harborview Security + GRC to review evidence artifacts and close open items next week.
next_steps: Redwood to send evidence pack: example audit logs + image signing/SBOM notes + change-management template.
Customer to share internal control requirements for production changes (CAB vs lightweight approval).
Schedule follow-up security review and optionally include Harborview’s SIEM owner to discuss log export format.
transcript:
Meeting: Security review: Dedicated provisioning (image provenance, audit logs, change management)
Recorded by Fireflies.ai
Date: 2025-03-06
Duration: 47 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Lauren Bishop, Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei, Vanessa Ortiz
Harborview Financial Services: Dina Patel, Markus Engel, Hannah Cho, Omar Nasser


[00:00] Lauren Bishop: Alright, cool. Thanks everybody for making time. The agenda we had was basically image provenance, audit logging around provisioning actions, and then change-management expectations for Dedicated expansions.

[00:12] Dina Patel: Yep. That’s right. We’re basically trying to map this to our internal controls. We can move fast but we need evidence, right, and we need to know what’s auditable.

[00:23] Lauren Bishop: Totally. I’ll do a quick framing and then Marcus and Kevin can go deep. Vanessa’s here from the fleet automation effort.

[00:34] Omar Nasser: Great.

[00:36] Lauren Bishop: So context: you’re looking at Dedicated capacity in, was it us-east and eu-west, right?

[00:42] Markus Engel: Correct. Initial would be us-east-1 equivalent, then later Frankfurt.

[00:48] Lauren Bishop: Okay. Dedicated for us means physically isolated GPU pools, separate tenancy at the cluster level, and routing only sends your org traffic to that capacity once it’s marked Ready in our control plane.

[01:03] Hannah Cho: When you say Ready, is that like infra exists or like validated?

[01:08] Vanessa Ortiz: Validated. Not just “it booted.” We have a series of checks and then only after those pass it transitions to Ready.

[01:18] Dina Patel: Good, because we had some vendors that considered “ready” to mean “it created the nodes.”

[01:23] Lauren Bishop: Yeah, we don’t want that either.

[01:27] Lauren Bishop: Marcus, do you want to start with the image story?

[01:31] Marcus Lin: Sure. So we run a “golden image” pipeline for GPU nodes. The goal is deterministic base OS + pinned driver stack + runtime prerequisites, with controlled promotion from build to staging to prod.

[01:46] Marcus Lin: On provenance: we sign the artifacts and we produce an SBOM. We also have build metadata we can provide—basically the “who built it, from what source, when.”

[01:59] Dina Patel: When you say sign artifacts, are we talking like AMIs signed? Or containers? Or both?

[02:05] Marcus Lin: Both patterns exist. For node images, it depends on the substrate. If it’s a cloud image, we use the cloud-native mechanisms plus our own signing of the build output. For containers and charts, we sign those too. For the purpose of this call, we can focus on the node image and the provisioning configs.

[02:23] Markus Engel: And can we verify those signatures ourselves? Like independently?

[02:28] Marcus Lin: Yes. We can share the public verification info and the process. We typically use cosign-like flows for container artifacts and attestations. For node images, verification is a bit more nuanced depending on provider, but we can still provide attestations and checksums that you can validate.

[02:47] Hannah Cho: Do you align to SLSA? We have a control that references SLSA level, not strictly required but asked.

[02:54] Marcus Lin: We’re not going to claim a specific SLSA level on this call, because it’s easy to overstate. What we can say is we generate build provenance attestations and SBOMs, and we enforce restricted promotion—meaning not every engineer can promote an image to production. Those actions are logged.

[03:13] Kevin Osei: And to tie it back, the promotion itself shows up in our audit logs as a change event.

[03:18] Dina Patel: Okay. So the evidence we’d like is: sample attestation, sample SBOM, and then a description of the keys and how they’re protected.

[03:27] Marcus Lin: Yep. We can provide that.

[03:30] Omar Nasser: What about kernel params and like, the whole GPU driver story? We’ve had issues with vendors upgrading drivers under us.

[03:38] Vanessa Ortiz: We pin drivers by image version. So each golden image is versioned. We also pin the runtime chart versions in cluster bootstrap. The idea is that a pool bring-up references a specific image version and a specific runtime bundle version. Then you get deterministic behavior.

[03:55] Markus Engel: If there’s a CVE in the driver, do you force-update?

[04:00] Marcus Lin: We handle it like any security patch. We’ll build a new image and propose rollout. For Dedicated, we coordinate with you on a maintenance window unless it’s an emergency, and even then there’s a defined process.

[04:15] Hannah Cho: “Defined process” is the thing. We need to understand what “emergency” means and how it’s communicated.

[04:22] Lauren Bishop: Yep. We can share a change-management template that distinguishes scheduled vs emergency, and what notice we provide.

[04:31] Dina Patel: Okay. Now audit logs: can we shift to that?

[04:34] Lauren Bishop: Yep. Kevin, do you want to lead?

[04:37] Kevin Osei: Sure. So we have two classes of logs relevant here. One: provisioning workflow events—stage start/finish/failure, correlation IDs, and who initiated. Two: administrative audit logs—privileged actions like “break-glass override used” or “pause/resume provisioning run.”

[04:58] Kevin Osei: For each provisioning run, there’s a run ID, the pool ID, region, SKU, and timestamps per stage. Stages are like Requested, Provisioning, Imaging, Bootstrapping, Validating, Ready.

[05:14] Dina Patel: And who shows up as “initiated by”? A person, a service account, what?

[05:19] Kevin Osei: If triggered through our operator CLI or API, it’s an authenticated principal. Usually it’s a Redwood operator, but we record the user identity plus the originating service. If it’s an automated retry, you’ll see it as the provisioning service with a reference back to the original run.

[05:39] Markus Engel: Are these logs immutable?

[05:42] Kevin Osei: We treat them as append-only events. They’re shipped to our central logging with restricted write permissions. We can provide retention details and, for Dedicated enterprise customers, we can export a subset to your destination.

[05:58] Dina Patel: When you say export, do you mean like Splunk?

[06:01] Kevin Osei: Splunk HEC is common. Also syslog or S3-based exports depending on your preference. We’ll need to confirm what Harborview prefers.

[06:12] Omar Nasser: We use Splunk, but for some systems it’s S3 then ingestion.

[06:16] Dina Patel: Yeah, and we’d want fields normalized. Like action, actor, target, timestamp, outcome.

[06:24] Kevin Osei: That maps cleanly. We have structured JSON events. We can send sample payloads so you see the schema.

[06:33] Hannah Cho: Does it include “what changed”? Like config diff?

[06:38] Kevin Osei: We include references to the config version and validation results. For diffs, we can include a link or an identifier. We try to avoid dumping giant diffs into logs, but we can provide a canonical config hash and the versioned artifact ID.

[06:55] Vanessa Ortiz: And for config validation, there’s a policy gate step. That generates a “validation report” with pass/fail and rule IDs.

[07:04] Dina Patel: I heard “break-glass.” What does that mean in your system?

[07:08] Vanessa Ortiz: It’s an override mechanism if validation blocks a legit edge case. But it’s restricted.

[07:14] Kevin Osei: Restricted to admin-only principals. When it’s used, it generates an audit event and we can alert on it. Think of it like “override = true” with a required reason string.

[07:27] Dina Patel: Do you require approval? Like two-person rule?

[07:31] Marcus Lin: Not everywhere yet. Some orgs implement a two-person approval workflow; we have a lightweight version internally where break-glass requires an on-call + a second approver in Slack. But I want to be careful: the current productized mechanism is admin-only plus auditing and alerting. We can discuss aligning to your needs contractually.

[07:55] Hannah Cho: For compliance we don’t strictly need two-person, but we need that it’s reviewed and documented.

[08:02] Lauren Bishop: That’s consistent with what we’ve seen. We can propose “break-glass review within 24 hours,” something like that.

[08:10] Markus Engel: Another question: who at Redwood can actually touch the nodes? Like SSH.

[08:16] Marcus Lin: In Dedicated, we minimize direct host access. Operationally, most work is via the control plane and Kubernetes. Host-level access is restricted to a small on-call group with just-in-time access, and actions are logged. We can provide the overview.

[08:36] Dina Patel: Is it like bastion with session recording?

[08:39] Marcus Lin: For some environments, yes, there’s session recording. Again, details depend on where it’s deployed. But the principle is least privilege, short-lived credentials, and audit logging.

[08:53] Omar Nasser: So for the provisioning pipeline itself—what’s the change-management story? We’re mostly concerned about “you change the cluster under us.”

[09:02] Lauren Bishop: Right. So expansions and upgrades are treated as changes. For expansions, we schedule a window even if the expectation is “no downtime,” because we still want clear comms and rollback points.

[09:16] Lauren Bishop: The new automation we’re rolling out is meant to reduce variability and make those changes more predictable. It has readiness gates: smoke tests, network checks, GPU health checks, and a small performance canary run before Ready.

[09:34] Markus Engel: What does the perf canary do? Does it run our workloads?

[09:38] Vanessa Ortiz: It’s a lightweight benchmark suite. It uses a standard prompt set and measures throughput/latency on the new pool. It does not run your proprietary prompts unless we configure that as part of a separate eval.

[09:54] Dina Patel: Does that benchmark generate logs? Any risk of leaking data?

[09:58] Vanessa Ortiz: No customer data in the default. It’s synthetic. It generates a summary JSON like pass/fail and a few metrics.

[10:07] Hannah Cho: And change-management: are you notifying us when you build a new image? Or only when you roll it out?

[10:14] Lauren Bishop: We’d notify for rollouts that impact your pool. Building an image internally doesn’t necessarily impact you until we promote and deploy it.

[10:23] Dina Patel: We’d need at least like 7 days notice for planned changes. For emergency, we need immediate notice and a post-change report.

[10:33] Lauren Bishop: That’s consistent with our enterprise posture. We can put that into the comms plan.

[10:41] Kevin Osei: And we can provide a change event log entry that includes “planned window,” “executed at,” “rollback invoked yes/no.”

[10:52] Markus Engel: Can you roll back an image if it causes issues?

[10:56] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes, the whole point of versioned images is you can revert. There are some caveats if the underlying vendor deprecates something, but generally yes. For a pool, you can drain/replace nodes and roll back to a prior image version.

[11:14] Omar Nasser: Do you do in-place upgrades or replace nodes?

[11:17] Vanessa Ortiz: Replace. We treat nodes as immutable. It’s safer.

[11:23] Dina Patel: That is a green flag.

[11:26] Lauren Bishop: Great.

[11:28] Hannah Cho: On audit logs again: do we get access to your internal ticketing evidence? Like, we might need to show an auditor that changes were approved.

[11:38] Lauren Bishop: We can provide an export of relevant change records. Typically it’s a customer-facing change log plus the audit event stream and, if needed, a summary from our internal system. We wouldn’t expose full internal tickets by default, but we can provide the necessary evidence.

[11:58] Dina Patel: That’s fine. We don’t need your whole Jira.

[12:03] Kevin Osei: Another thing: the provisioning pipeline emits correlation IDs. So if a change triggers a provisioning run, you can trace the chain: request → stages → ready marking → routing advertise.

[12:17] Markus Engel: That “routing advertise” step is important. We want assurance that capacity doesn’t get traffic until validation passes.

[12:24] Vanessa Ortiz: That’s a hard gate. Routing only uses Ready. There was some debate early on about using Validating, but we decided against it.

[12:34] Omar Nasser: So if validation fails, what happens? Are nodes destroyed?

[12:39] Vanessa Ortiz: Depends on failure. If it’s a GPU health issue, we can auto-replace the node. If it’s misconfiguration, it stays out of routing and the run marks Failed with a reason. Operators can re-run only the validation stage after correcting config.

[12:58] Dina Patel: That implies operators can change config. Is that controlled?

[13:03] Kevin Osei: Config changes are versioned and validated. There are policy checks. Changes are limited by RBAC. And again, those actions are audit logged.

[13:15] Hannah Cho: Are audit logs retained for at least one year?

[13:19] Kevin Osei: Default retention is less than that in some systems, but for enterprise Dedicated we support longer retention. Let’s capture your requirement and we’ll align.

[13:30] Dina Patel: We need 400 days for certain systems. But we can also ingest to Splunk and retain ourselves.

[13:36] Kevin Osei: Great. Export solves it.

[13:39] Markus Engel: You mentioned the provisioning service. Is it a CI pipeline or a service?

[13:44] Vanessa Ortiz: It’s an internal service orchestrating the workflow, with persisted state transitions and retries. It calls Terraform modules, image hooks, bootstrap, and then validation.

[13:58] Markus Engel: Terraform has been a source of drift for us with other vendors.

[14:02] Vanessa Ortiz: We have drift detection too—desired versus actual settings and it surfaces drift in the control plane. That’s more operational, but it’s also relevant to audit.

[14:15] Dina Patel: Drift detection output, is that visible to customers?

[14:19] Lauren Bishop: We can provide visibility at the pool level: “compliant / drift detected” and some detail. Full internal details might be limited, but we can share what matters.

[14:31] Omar Nasser: Okay. Let’s talk about “image hardening” specifics. Are you CIS baselined? Do you disable password auth? Stuff like that.

[14:40] Marcus Lin: Yes—basic OS hardening: no password SSH, restricted inbound, minimal packages, patching cadence, and we scan images. GPU nodes have some extra considerations due to drivers. We can share a checklist excerpt.

[14:56] Dina Patel: Are you using FIPS anywhere?

[14:59] Marcus Lin: In some environments we can align to FIPS requirements, but it depends on the stack and provider. We should treat that as a separate deep dive. For this call: we can confirm encryption in transit and at rest, KMS integration, and key rotation.

[15:16] Hannah Cho: Our requirement is encryption at rest with customer-managed keys for certain datasets. Does Dedicated support that?

[15:22] Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated, data is isolated, and for some storage components we can integrate with your KMS. For the inference payload itself, we don’t persist prompts by default. Logs can be configured.

[15:37] Dina Patel: We mostly care about audit logs and system logs not containing sensitive prompts.

[15:42] Kevin Osei: We can configure redaction and we have controls to avoid logging payloads. For provisioning logs, there should be no customer payload by design.

[15:52] Omar Nasser: Are there any cases where your readiness checks make an actual model call with sample text?

[15:58] Vanessa Ortiz: Yes, but it’s synthetic and not your data. It’s like “Hello world” type prompts to confirm runtime responds and TLS is correct.

[16:08] Markus Engel: Understood.

[16:10] Dina Patel: Can you talk about who approves a capacity expansion? Like, do you have a CAB? Or is it just an engineer doing it?

[16:19] Lauren Bishop: For customer-initiated expansions, we treat it as a scheduled change. There’s a request record, an owner, and a planned window. Internally it’s reviewed by the infra on-point. For regulated customers, we can add a more formal approval chain.

[16:37] Hannah Cho: We don’t need a formal CAB on your side, but we do need you to show “this was approved per process.”

[16:44] Lauren Bishop: That’s reasonable.

[16:47] Kevin Osei: From an audit perspective, we can show: request created, provisioning run triggered by principal X, validations passed, capacity marked Ready, and routing began sending traffic. That chain is what auditors usually want.

[17:03] Dina Patel: Exactly.

[17:05] Omar Nasser: One more on signing: do you publish a public key? Or is it internal?

[17:10] Marcus Lin: For verification, we can provide the public verification material. We can also provide a statement of how keys are stored (HSM / KMS-backed) and rotation policy.

[17:23] Markus Engel: And are the images built in a separate account? Like isolated build env?

[17:28] Marcus Lin: Yes, build pipeline runs in a controlled environment with restricted permissions. We’re moving toward stronger separation as part of the hardening work.

[17:40] Dina Patel: Okay. This is good. The thing we need is evidence artifacts, not just “yes.”

[17:46] Lauren Bishop: Totally fair.

[17:48] Vanessa Ortiz: Also, just to be explicit: the new automation work is adding more structured events and better auditing around stage transitions. So what we’ll send you will look like the events we use ourselves.

[18:03] Dina Patel: Perfect.

[18:05] Hannah Cho: And what about notice when you use break-glass? Would we get notified?

[18:11] Kevin Osei: We can configure alerting for break-glass usage and notify your named contacts. At minimum it’s logged and reviewed internally.

[18:21] Lauren Bishop: We can put that in the change template: “break-glass used” triggers immediate notice.

[18:27] Markus Engel: Great.

[18:29] Omar Nasser: Slight pivot—do you have SOC 2? ISO?

[18:34] Marcus Lin: Yes, we have SOC 2 Type II. ISO coverage depends on the specific scope; we can share our current compliance pack.

[18:44] Dina Patel: We’ll ask for the report under NDA. Not today.

[18:48] Lauren Bishop: Yep.

[18:50] Markus Engel: Competitors: we also talked to Bedrock and Vertex. Their story is “it’s managed,” but we can’t get the control we need.

[18:58] Lauren Bishop: Understood. Dedicated gives you predictable capacity plus the controls we’re discussing. We also see folks look at Together or others for dedicated GPU, but the enterprise controls vary.

[19:13] Dina Patel: Yeah. The key is auditability and change control.

[19:18] Kevin Osei: One more technical detail: we can provide stage timing metrics too. It’s not a security requirement but it helps you understand how long expansions take and where delays happen.

[19:28] Omar Nasser: Actually that matters. We don’t want a 3-day window with unknown status.

[19:34] Vanessa Ortiz: That’s exactly why we built this pipeline. It posts progress updates and dashboards. You’ll have visibility like “Imaging 12 minutes,” “Bootstrapping 20 minutes,” etc.

[19:49] Markus Engel: Are those dashboards customer-visible?

[19:52] Lauren Bishop: Today, some are internal. For enterprise customers we can share a customer-friendly view or status updates. We can talk about what you want.

[20:03] Dina Patel: Even just structured status updates during a change window would be fine.

[20:09] Lauren Bishop: Great.

[20:12] Hannah Cho: Could we get a list of what fields are in audit logs? Like a schema doc.

[20:17] Kevin Osei: Yep. I’ll send sample payloads and a field list.

[20:22] Dina Patel: And also: who in Redwood has permission to trigger a provisioning run. That’s part of our vendor access review.

[20:30] Marcus Lin: We’ll include that in the access control overview. It’s restricted to the infra fleet team and a limited on-call rotation, with admin actions separated.

[20:43] Omar Nasser: Okay. What about change windows: do you do them in our business hours?

[20:49] Lauren Bishop: We can align to your preference. Some customers prefer weekends. For expansions specifically, we can often do it with no traffic impact, but we still schedule a time when both sides can monitor.

[21:03] Markus Engel: If it’s truly no impact, could it be outside hours and we just get a report?

[21:09] Lauren Bishop: Potentially. For the first one, we’d recommend monitored.

[21:13] Dina Patel: Agree.

[21:15] Kevin Osei: Also, to clarify: “no impact” assumes we keep the pool out of routing until Ready. That’s the safe posture.

[21:24] Dina Patel: Right.

[21:26] Hannah Cho: Do you have a post-change report template?

[21:30] Lauren Bishop: We can create one. It can include: what changed (image version, runtime version), validation results, any incidents, and confirmation of success.

[21:42] Markus Engel: Nice.

[21:45] Dina Patel: Okay. I think we have what we need. Can we do a recap and next steps?

[21:51] Lauren Bishop: Yep. Let me summarize and you tell me if I missed anything.

[21:56] Lauren Bishop: One: Redwood will send sample audit log events for provisioning, including actor, stage transitions, Ready marking, and break-glass usage. Two: Marcus will send image provenance details—signing, SBOM format, and a hardening checklist excerpt, plus how to verify signatures. Three: we’ll propose a change-management template with notice periods, emergency process, and a post-change report.

[22:21] Lauren Bishop: On your side: confirm log export preference (Splunk HEC vs S3), and confirm retention requirements. Then we schedule a follow-up with security and GRC to review the evidence pack.

[22:34] Dina Patel: That’s accurate.

[22:36] Hannah Cho: Yes.

[22:38] Omar Nasser: Works for me.

[22:40] Markus Engel: Same.

[22:42] Kevin Osei: Great. I’ll send the sample payloads early next week.

[22:47] Marcus Lin: And I’ll get you the provenance notes and key handling overview.

[22:52] Lauren Bishop: Perfect. Thanks all.

[22:55] Dina Patel: Thanks.

[22:56] Fireflies.ai: Meeting ended.

Note: Recording contained additional small talk and scheduling details after the recap; Fireflies truncation removed ~1-2 minutes of low-content audio.
